ii4rg6:554: The most important architectural problem in today's AI infrastructure is not which model to use, but how much infrastructure is needed to build something truly useful with it. Anthropic, OpenAI, CrewAI, and LangChain all call the layer that wraps the agent a harness. The harness includes the orchestration loop, tools (MCP, A2A), memory, context management, and error handling—things that make the model useful. They all agree that the model itself is not the product; the infrastructure is. But they deeply disagree on how heavyweight this infrastructure layer should be. Anthropic's harness is thin. It is an elegant loop: assemble the prompt, call the model, execute tool calls, and repeat. Everything is decided by the model. OpenAI adds more structure: instruction stacks, orchestration patterns, and explicit handoff patterns. CrewAI takes a multi-pronged approach: using deterministic Flows for routing and validation, leaving the rest to autonomous agents. LangGraph's harness is the heaviest—every decision is a node, every transition is a defined edge, and the entire workflow is encoded in the harness. On one end of this spectrum, you have strong trust in the model and weak encoding of logic; on the other end, weak trust in the model and strong encoding of logic. Every team building systems with agents must choose how large a harness they need. But buried in this debate is an assumption no one questions: the harness lives outside the traditional backend.
